glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: By offering His own body once for all, Jesus accomplished what the law’s repeated sacrifices never could, perfecting forever those who are being sanctified; so believers are to draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another, take seriously the warning against rejecting the Son, and keep their confidence until He comes.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 10:1–18 completes the teaching on Christ’s priesthood and sacrifice that began at 4:14. At 10:19 the book’s fourth movement begins, turning that teaching into a call to draw near and endure.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” (Hebrews 10:22)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The law’s yearly sacrifices only reminded people of their sins, “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins” (10:4). So the Son came saying, “a body You have prepared for Me” (10:5), and He offered that body once for all to do God’s will. Israel’s priests stood day after day, but Jesus offered one sacrifice and sat down. “For by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified” (10:14). Through Jeremiah the Spirit adds God’s promise to remember their sins no more, and where sins are forgiven, no further offering is needed (10:17–18).

On that foundation Hebrews makes its great appeal. Believers have boldness to enter God’s presence “by the blood of Jesus,” through “a new and living way” opened through His flesh, and they have a High Priest over God’s house (10:19–21). So, “let us draw near,” “let us hold fast,” and “let us consider one another,” gathering to stir up love and good works as the Day approaches (10:22–25).

Then comes a solemn warning, addressed to the whole congregation with the writer included: “if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,” only “a certain fearful expectation of judgment” (10:26–27). Hebrews describes this willful sin as trampling the Son of God underfoot, insulting the Spirit of grace, and treating as common “the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified” (10:29). “Sanctified” here means set apart for God; the writer does not say whether that setting apart had involved inward renewal. The only sacrifice that forgives is the one rejected. The writer at once reminds his hearers of their earlier endurance and urges them not to throw away their confidence: “we are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul” (10:39).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 10:1–4 — A Shadow That Could Not Take Away Sins

The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, so its sacrifices, repeated year after year, could never make worshipers perfect. They brought a yearly reminder of sin, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sin away.

Hebrews 10:5–10 — A Body Prepared to Do God’s Will

Coming into the world, the Son speaks Psalm 40: God prepared a body for Him, and He came to do God’s will. He sets aside the sacrifices the law required, and through the offering of His own body once for all, believers are made holy.

Hebrews 10:11–14 — One Sacrifice, and He Sat Down

Israel’s priests stand every day offering sacrifices that can never remove sins, but Jesus offered one sacrifice for sins forever and sat down at God’s right hand. By that single offering He has perfected forever those who are being made holy.

Hebrews 10:15–18 — The Spirit Witnesses to Forgiveness

The Holy Spirit confirms this through Jeremiah’s promise that God will write His laws on His people’s hearts and remember their sins no more. Where sins are forgiven, no more offering for sin is needed.

Hebrews 10:19–25 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another

Because Jesus’ blood has opened a new and living way into God’s presence and He serves as High Priest over God’s house, believers can draw near with full assurance, cleansed in heart and body. They must hold fast their hope, because God is faithful, and keep meeting together to spur one another on to love and good works as the Day approaches.

Hebrews 10:26–31 — No Sacrifice Left for Willful Rejection

Those who received the knowledge of the truth and then deliberately reject Christ have no sacrifice left for their sins, only a terrifying expectation of judgment. If rejecting Moses’ law brought death, far worse punishment awaits those who trample the Son of God, treat as common the covenant blood by which they were set apart, and insult the Spirit of grace.

Hebrews 10:32–39 — Do Not Cast Away Your Confidence

The hearers are to remember how they once endured public suffering, stood with others who suffered, and joyfully accepted the loss of their goods because they had a better, lasting possession. They must not throw away their confidence but endure, for Christ is coming, and they are among those who believe to the saving of the soul.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 10 shows that Christ’s sacrifice is finished. One offering has dealt with sin forever, and God remembers forgiven sins no more (10:14, 17). Believers do not need to keep offering anything to be accepted. They can draw near with full assurance and a cleansed conscience.

The chapter also shows that this confidence is meant to be lived together and held to the end. Believers draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another, especially as the Day approaches (10:22–25). The warning of 10:26–31 describes deliberate, settled rejection of Christ, not the struggle of a believer who keeps coming back to Him. For those who are fearful or failing, the invitation of 10:19–22 stands open.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Shadow and reality. The law’s repeated sacrifices could not take away sins (10:1–4, 11).

A body prepared. The Son came to do God’s will and offered His own body once for all (10:5–10).

Perfected forever. One offering perfects those who are being sanctified, and God remembers their sins no more (10:12–18).

Draw near together. Believers draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another (10:19–25).

Warning and confidence. Willful rejection of Christ leaves no sacrifice, while persevering faith leads to salvation (10:26–39).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
A body You have prepared (10:5). Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 in the Greek form many Jewish communities used. The body is Jesus’ own, in which He came to do God’s will and which He offered once for all.

Sanctified (10:10, 14). Set apart for God and made holy. Believers are sanctified through Christ’s offering, and God continues that work in them.

Sat down (10:12). Israel’s priests always stood because their work was never done. Jesus sat down because His sacrifice was complete, though He continues to intercede for His people (7:25).

The new and living way (10:20). The way into God’s presence that Jesus opened through His own flesh, given in death, replacing the closed veil of the tabernacle.

Sin willfully (10:26). Hebrews defines this in 10:29 as settled, defiant rejection of Christ: trampling the Son of God, treating as common the covenant blood by which the person was sanctified, or set apart, and insulting the Spirit of grace.

“The just shall live by faith” (10:38). Words from Habakkuk 2:4. God’s righteous people live by trusting Him while they wait for the One who is coming, and this verse leads into the examples of faith in chapter 11.

focus: Hebrews 10 completes the argument that Jesus’ single offering of His own body accomplished what the law’s repeated sacrifices never could, perfecting forever those who are being sanctified and bringing the forgiveness Jeremiah promised. On that basis the chapter calls believers to draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another, warns gravely against willful rejection of the Son, and urges them to remember their earlier endurance and keep their confidence until He comes.

sections.title: A Shadow That Could Not Take Away Sins
sections.summary: The law has only a shadow of the good things to come, so its sacrifices, offered year by year, can never make worshipers perfect; if they could, they would have ceased. Instead they bring a reminder of sins every year, “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4).

sections.title: A Body Prepared to Do God’s Will
sections.summary: Coming into the world, the Son speaks the words of Psalm 40 in the Greek form Hebrews quotes: “a body You have prepared for Me” (Hebrews 10:5) and “Behold, I have come to do Your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:9). He takes away the first, the sacrifices offered according to the law, to establish the second, the doing of God’s will through the offering of His own body, and by that will “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10).

sections.title: One Sacrifice, and He Sat Down
sections.summary: Every priest stands daily offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins, but Jesus offered one sacrifice for sins forever and sat down at the right hand of God, waiting till His enemies are made His footstool. “For by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14).

sections.title: The Spirit Witnesses to Forgiveness
sections.summary: The Holy Spirit bears witness through Jeremiah’s promise that God will put His laws into His people’s hearts and write them in their minds, and that He will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more. “Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18).

sections.title: Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
sections.summary: Having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus, through the new and living way He consecrated through the veil of His flesh, and having a High Priest over the house of God, believers are to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, their hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and their bodies washed with pure water. They are to hold fast the confession of their hope, for He who promised is faithful, and to consider one another to stir up love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of themselves together as they see the Day approaching.

sections.title: No Sacrifice Left for Willful Rejection
sections.summary: If we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains, only a fearful expectation of judgment. If rejecting Moses’ law brought death, much worse punishment awaits the one who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace, for “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

sections.title: Do Not Cast Away Your Confidence
sections.summary: The hearers are to recall the former days when they endured public reproach, stood with those who suffered, and joyfully accepted the plundering of their goods, knowing they had a better and enduring possession in heaven. “Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has great reward” (Hebrews 10:35), for He who is coming will come, and “we are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul” (Hebrews 10:39).

1.brief: The law has only “a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things,” so its repeated yearly sacrifices can never make worshipers perfect. A shadow points to something real but cannot supply it.
1.explain: “a shadow of the good things to come” The law’s sacrifices outlined what God would provide in Christ. Their yearly repetition shows that the outline could never bring worshipers to the goal of complete cleansing and lasting access. What the shadow anticipates must be accomplished by the offering itself.

2.brief: If those sacrifices could have truly cleansed the worshipers, they would have stopped being offered, for the worshipers, once purified, “would have had no more consciousness of sins.” The constant repetition proves that the sacrifices did not finish the work.
2.explain: “would they not have ceased to be offered” A sacrifice that finally purified the worshipers would have ended the need for another. Having no more consciousness of sins means no continuing burden of guilt requiring another offering. The continuing cycle tells the writer that the old sacrifices had not finished that work.

3.brief: Instead, those sacrifices brought “a reminder of sins every year.” Each Day of Atonement reminded Israel that sin had not been finally removed.
3.explain: “a reminder of sins every year” The annual sacrifices brought Israel’s sins to mind again. The people were reminded of the need for atonement every time that offering returned. The yearly reminder prepares for God’s promise in verse 17 to remember their sins no more.

4.brief: “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins.” Animal blood could point to forgiveness, but it could never remove sin itself.
4.explain: “the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins” God gave the animal sacrifices their place in Israel’s worship. Their blood could never accomplish the final removal of human sin. The next verse answers that limitation by bringing the Son and His offering into view.

5.brief: When the Son came into the world, He spoke the words of Psalm 40 in the Greek form Hebrews quotes: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, But a body You have prepared for Me.” God prepared a human body for His Son, the body in which He would do God’s will and offer Himself.
5.explain: “a body You have prepared for Me” Hebrews puts Psalm 40 on the Son’s lips as He comes into the world. God had provided Jesus with His own human body, in which He came to obey and which He would give as the sacrifice. The opening words about offering prepare for the contrast between the earlier sacrifices and the Son who gives Himself.
5.notes: The ancient Greek wording of Psalm 40 quoted by Hebrews speaks of a prepared body. In Psalm 40:6 the NKJV, translated from the Hebrew, speaks of opened ears. Both images accompany the speaker’s readiness to do God’s will.

6.brief: The Son continues, “In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin You had no pleasure.” The animal offerings did not satisfy God; what pleased Him was the Son coming in a prepared body to do His will.
6.explain: “In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin You had no pleasure” The Son continues the psalm’s address to God. Burnt offerings and sin offerings had an appointed place, yet God’s saving purpose calls for the obedience and self-offering of the Son that follows.

7.brief: The Son then says, “Behold, I have come— In the volume of the book it is written of Me— To do Your will, O God.” Jesus came in fulfillment of Scripture to carry out the Father’s will completely.
7.explain: “To do Your will, O God” The Son presents Himself as the One who has come to carry out God’s will. The scroll points to the written word that speaks of His coming. The focus falls on the will He comes to do, fulfilled in offering His prepared body.

8.brief: Hebrews notes that the sacrifices God did not desire or delight in were the very ones “offered according to the law.” Although the law itself required these offerings, God took no pleasure in them as the final answer to sin, and this prepares for the Son who comes to do His will.
8.explain: “which are offered according to the law” Hebrews gathers the kinds of sacrifices just named and stresses that they were lawful offerings. Their limitation is part of the argument about the order God gave, not a charge that worshipers had invented the sacrifices. The decisive change comes with the Son’s obedient offering.

9.brief: Then the Son says, “Behold, I have come to do Your will, O God,” and in this way “He takes away the first that He may establish the second.” The sacrifices the law required give way to the Son’s obedient offering of His own body in doing God’s will.
9.explain: “He takes away the first that He may establish the second” The first is the order of offerings named in verse 8. The second is the doing of God’s will that the Son announces. Jesus establishes that second order through His obedient self-offering.

10.brief: “By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” Believers are set apart for God by Jesus’ single offering of His own body, an offering that never needs to be repeated.
10.explain: “we have been sanctified” God’s will is carried out through the offering of Jesus’ own body. On the strength of that once-for-all offering God has set His people apart for Himself. Their standing comes from what Christ has done on their behalf.

11.brief: Every priest stands daily, offering the same sacrifices again and again, sacrifices “which can never take away sins.” The standing priests and their repeated offerings show that the work was never finished.
11.explain: “every priest stands ministering daily” The priest keeps standing to serve, and the same sacrifices keep returning. The fact that these offerings cannot take away sins explains why the routine does not come to completion. The Son’s seated position in the next verse makes the contrast visible.

12.brief: “But this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God.” Jesus sat down because His sacrifice was complete, in sharp contrast to the priests who kept standing.
12.explain: “one sacrifice for sins forever” Jesus offered one sacrifice and took His seat at God’s right hand. His action shows that His offering for sins is complete and its effect endures. He remains the living Priest who represents His people, as Hebrews 7:25 has already said.

13.brief: From that time Jesus is waiting “till His enemies are made His footstool.” His seat at God’s right hand looks forward to the full subjection of every enemy, as Psalm 110 promised.
13.explain: “His enemies are made His footstool” Psalm 110:1 pictures the full subjection of the Son’s enemies. He waits for that completion from His place at God’s right hand. His sacrifice is already finished, and the visible defeat of all opposition still lies ahead.

14.brief: “For by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.” Jesus’ single offering gives His people a complete and lasting standing before God, even as God continues His sanctifying work in them.
14.explain: “He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified” The single offering has brought its people to the intended goal of a lasting standing before God. The same sentence speaks of them as people still being made holy. Christ’s finished work gives security while God’s ongoing work forms them in holiness.

15.brief: The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us, Hebrews says, speaking through the words of Jeremiah. The Spirit testifies that Christ’s one offering has truly perfected those who are being sanctified, as the promise quoted next confirms.
15.explain: “the Holy Spirit also witnesses to us” The writer brings Jeremiah’s covenant promise back as the Holy Spirit’s present testimony. The sentence carries the reader into verses 16–17, where God Himself speaks about inward obedience and lasting forgiveness.

16.brief: God promised, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the LORD: I will put My laws into their hearts, and in their minds I will write them.” God places His instruction within His people so that obedience comes from within, and Jeremiah joins this inward change to the forgiveness that the one offering secures.
16.explain: “I will put My laws into their hearts” God promises to give His instruction an inward home in His people’s hearts and minds. He takes responsibility for the change the covenant requires. This inward work is one half of the promise the Spirit uses to bear witness to Christ’s completed offering.

17.brief: Then God adds, “Their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more.” This promise of full forgiveness is the testimony Hebrews has been building toward.
17.explain: “I will remember no more” God pledges to forgive His people’s sins and lawless deeds so that He no longer holds them against them. This is the lasting answer to the yearly remembrance of sins in verse 3.

18.brief: “Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.” Since God has fully forgiven sins through Christ, no further sacrifice for sin is needed.
18.explain: “there is no longer an offering for sin” Remission means forgiveness. Once sins are forgiven on the strength of Christ’s completed offering, another sacrifice for those sins is unnecessary. That conclusion supplies the ground for the bold approach called for next.

19.brief: Therefore believers have “boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus.” The confidence to come into God’s very presence rests on Jesus’ blood, not on the worshiper’s own worthiness.
19.explain: “boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus” Everything just said about forgiveness leads to a changed approach to God. The Holiest names the presence to which access was once so restricted. Jesus’ blood gives the congregation freedom to enter with confidence.

20.brief: Jesus opened “a new and living way” for His people through the veil, “that is, His flesh.” His body given in death has opened the way into God’s presence that the tabernacle veil once closed.
20.explain: “through the veil, that is, His flesh” Jesus opened a new and living way by giving His body. Hebrews identifies the veil with His flesh here so the tabernacle image can explain how His death gives access. The way stays open through the living Priest who secured it.

21.brief: Believers also have “a High Priest over the house of God.” Jesus not only opened the way but continues to serve as High Priest over God’s people.
21.explain: “a High Priest over the house of God” The opened way belongs with the living Priest who presides over God’s people. Hebrews gives both grounds before asking the church to draw near: Jesus’ blood has opened the way, and Jesus Himself serves there on their behalf.

22.brief: “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” The sprinkling and washing recall how priests were prepared for service in Exodus 29:4 and Exodus 29:21 and God’s promise to cleanse His people in Ezekiel 36:25–26, and because Christ cleanses the whole person, guilty conscience included, believers can draw near in full assurance.
22.explain: “in full assurance of faith” A true heart comes to God sincerely, relying on what Christ has done. The sprinkling of hearts and washing of bodies recall priestly preparation (Exodus 29:4, 21 and Leviticus 16:4) and God’s promise to cleanse His people and give them a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–26). Through Christ a guilty conscience is cleansed and the whole person is made ready to draw near.
22.notes: Some readers also hear an echo of baptism in the bodily washing. The language fits a visible sign of the cleansing described in the sentence.

23.brief: “Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for He who promised is faithful.” Believers can hold firmly to their hope because the God who made the promise will keep it.
23.explain: “the confession of our hope without wavering” The church is to keep holding and confessing its hope even under pressure. God’s faithfulness is the reason the confession can remain firm. The certainty belongs to the promise because the One who made it will keep His word.

24.brief: “And let us consider one another in order to stir up love and good works.” Believers are to give thought to one another so that they encourage each other toward love and faithful action.
24.explain: “consider one another” Each believer is called to give thoughtful attention to others so that love and good works are stirred up. The command moves from holding one’s own confession to helping the rest of God’s household persevere in visible ways.

25.brief: Believers must not forsake assembling together, as some were doing, but must exhort one another, “and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.” Gathering and mutual encouragement grow more urgent as the Lord’s return draws near.
25.explain: “exhorting one another” Some had made a habit of leaving the gathering. Hebrews calls the rest to keep meeting and actively encouraging one another. The approach of the day of Christ’s return gives greater urgency to that mutual care.

26.brief: “For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” Turning deliberately away from Christ after knowing the truth leaves no other sacrifice, because His is the only one.
26.explain: “if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth” The writer includes himself in a warning to professing members who had received knowledge of the gospel. Verse 29 identifies the willful sin as settled, defiant rejection of Christ. The person who refuses His sacrifice refuses the only offering that takes away sin. The struggling believer who still seeks Christ has the open way described in verses 19–22.

27.brief: What remains instead is “a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and fiery indignation which will devour the adversaries.” Those who reject Christ’s sacrifice face God’s judgment as His enemies.
27.explain: “a certain fearful expectation of judgment” Where Christ’s sacrifice is rejected, what remains is God’s judgment. The fire that devours His adversaries describes the seriousness of standing against Him. Hebrews will describe drawing back as ending in ruin in verse 39.

28.brief: Anyone who rejected Moses’ law “dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Hebrews recalls how seriously the law treated deliberate rebellion.
28.explain: “on the testimony of two or three witnesses” Under Moses’ law, a proven act of covenant rebellion could bring death without mercy. Deuteronomy 17:2–7 supplies the setting and the requirement for witnesses. Hebrews uses that earlier accountability to prepare the comparison in verse 29.

29.brief: Much worse punishment is deserved by the one “who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace.” To treat the covenant blood that sanctified him as ordinary and worthless is to reject the very sacrifice that brings forgiveness, which is far graver than rejecting Moses’ law.
29.explain: “trampled the Son of God underfoot” The greater punishment corresponds to contempt for the Son, treating His covenant blood as common, and insulting the Spirit of grace. The person had been set apart by that blood in the sense the verse describes, and now treats it as ordinary. Hebrews leaves open whether that prior setting apart involved inward renewal. Its direct concern is what the person received and has willfully repudiated.

30.brief: “For we know Him who said, ‘Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,’ says the Lord. And again, ‘The LORD will judge His people.’” Hebrews grounds the warning in the character and word of God, who is the judge of His people.
30.explain: “The LORD will judge His people” The quotations draw on Deuteronomy 32:35–36. God claims the right to repay and to judge His people. The writer appeals to the God the congregation knows so that His warning is heard as an expression of His own authority and justice.

31.brief: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” The warning ends by calling the hearers to take God’s judgment with full seriousness.
31.explain: “fall into the hands of the living God” The living God Himself carries out the judgment just described. The fear belongs to being handed over to His judgment after rejecting His Son. The following appeal to remember earlier faithfulness gives the hearers a concrete reason to hold fast.

32.brief: The writer calls the hearers to recall the former days when, after they were enlightened, “you endured a great struggle with sufferings.” Remembering their earlier faithfulness is meant to strengthen them now.
32.explain: “after you were illuminated” The hearers can look back to the days after the gospel brought them light, when they endured a severe struggle. The writer calls them to remember an endurance they have already practiced and can show again.

33.brief: In those days the hearers were sometimes publicly exposed to insults and hardships, and at other times they stood alongside others who were treated the same way. They had suffered for Christ and stood with those who suffered.
33.explain: “you became companions of those who were so treated” Some sufferings were public: the hearers were exposed to insults and hardship. They also chose to stand beside others subjected to the same mistreatment. Their endurance was expressed both in bearing their own suffering and in sharing the cost of others’ suffering.

34.brief: In the NKJV the writer recalls their compassion “on me in my chains,” but the emphasis falls on the hearers, who cared for those who suffered and joyfully accepted the loss of their own property, knowing that they had “a better and an enduring possession” in heaven. Their compassion and endurance in loss came from confidence in a lasting treasure.
34.explain: “a better and an enduring possession for yourselves in heaven” The NKJV describes the congregation showing compassion to the writer in chains. They also accepted the seizure of their own goods with joy because they knew what God held for them. The better possession explains why the losses they suffered could not take away their hope.
34.notes: The NKJV follows the wording about the writer’s chains. Other manuscript witnesses speak of compassion for prisoners. Both readings preserve the emphasis on the hearers’ compassion, and the difference leaves the writer’s own imprisonment uncertain.

35.brief: “Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has great reward.” The confidence they showed before is still worth holding, because God will richly reward it.
35.explain: “do not cast away your confidence” The confidence that carried them through those losses is still theirs to hold. It has great reward because God stands behind what they trust. The warning is answered here by a direct appeal to remain confident.

36.brief: The hearers “have need of endurance,” so that after doing God’s will they may receive what He promised. Endurance is the bridge between obedience now and the promise later.
36.explain: “you have need of endurance” They have done God’s will through suffering and still need to keep doing it until the promise is received. The interval between obedience and fulfillment calls for continued faith, which the following quotation encourages.

37.brief: Hebrews quotes Habakkuk: “For yet a little while, And He who is coming will come and will not tarry.” Jesus is the One who is coming, and He will surely come without delay at the time God has set.
37.explain: “He who is coming will come and will not tarry” The promise gives an end to the wait: the coming One, Jesus, will surely arrive. The words about a little while put the delay under God’s appointment. They give the hearers reason to persevere without giving a calendar date.
37.notes: Hebrews draws on Habakkuk 2:3–4. The prophet was called to wait for the appointed fulfillment of God’s word. Hebrews uses the same language of certainty in speaking of the coming One.

38.brief: “Now the just shall live by faith; But if anyone draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him.” God’s righteous people live by trusting Him, while drawing back from that trust displeases Him.
38.explain: “the just shall live by faith” God’s righteous people live by continuing to trust Him. The second half warns that He takes no pleasure in drawing back. The quotation sets endurance and retreat before the congregation as genuinely different responses to what God has spoken.

39.brief: “But we are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul.” Drawing back from Christ leads to ruin, while persevering faith leads to salvation, and the writer is confident that he and his hearers belong among those who keep believing.
39.explain: “those who believe to the saving of the soul” Drawing back ends in perdition, or ruin. Persevering faith looks to salvation. The writer includes himself and expresses confidence that the congregation belongs with those who keep believing. That encouragement leads straight into the witnesses of faith in chapter 11.
